reason: Normal-curve shading shows why the conditional probability divides by the smaller region, and two tail areas show how the inverse-normal equations fix the mean and standard deviation.

scenes.title: Conditional probability as a fraction of the region above 220 g
scenes.purpose: See that knowing the wedge is over 220 g shrinks the sample space, so the tail above 260 g is divided by P(X > 220).

steps.text: The points of inflection sit at $\mu\pm\sigma$, so $\mu=230$ and $\sigma=18$. This is the first M1: the curve drawn is $\mathrm{N}(230,18^2)$.
The pale region is $\mathrm{P}(X>220)\approx 0.711$ and the dark region is $\mathrm{P}(X>260)\approx 0.0478$. Both probabilities are needed, which earns the first M1.

Given the wedge is over $220$ g, only the pale region is possible, so the answer is the dark part of it: $\frac{0.0478}{0.711}\approx 0.0672$. This is the second M1 and the A1. Dividing by $\mathrm{P}(X>260)$ or giving $0.0478$ alone is the conditional-denominator error.
Drag $k$ down to $225$: the dark region fills most of the pale region, so the conditional probability rises towards $1$. Dragging $k$ up makes it tiny.

guide.what_you_see: The bell-shaped density curve of the wedge mass $X$, with the whole region above $220$ g shaded palely and the region above the slider value $k$ shaded darker inside it. It shows the conditional probability as one tail divided by a larger region.

legend.meaning: The probability density function of $X$, the normal curve $\mathrm{N}(230,18^2)$ found from the question. The dashed-style line at $x=230$ marks the mean.
The left point of inflection of the curve, at $x=212$, which is $\mu-\sigma$.
The right point of inflection of the curve, at $x=248$, which is $\mu+\sigma$.
The pale region under the curve for $x>220$: the probability $\mathrm{P}(X>220)$, the wedge being over the labelled mass. It is the sample space once you know the label.
The darker region under the curve for $x>k$. At $k=260$ it is $\mathrm{P}(X>260)$, the event you want, and it lies wholly inside region $A$.

interact.do: Drag the slider between $225$ and $290$, starting at $260$. Try it at $260$, then drag it down towards $225$ and up towards $290$.
interact.watch: The darker region changes size and the reading $\mathrm{P}(X>k)$ changes with it. At $k=260$ it is about $0.0478$, so the ratio with $0.711$ is about $0.0672$. As $k$ falls to $225$ the dark region fills most of the pale one and the ratio rises towards $1$; as $k$ rises the ratio becomes tiny.

question_link.text: The inflection points $I_1$ and $I_2$ at $212$ and $248$ give $\mu=230$ and $\sigma=18$, which is the first M1 (finding $\mathrm{P}(X>260)$ or $\mathrm{P}(X>220)$). The dark region $B$ over the pale region $A$ is the conditional probability $\frac{\mathrm{P}(X>260)}{\mathrm{P}(X>220)}$ of the second M1, and its value $\approx 0.0672$ is the A1.

read_off: The live label $\mathrm{P}(X>220)$ is the area of the pale region $A$, about $0.711$. This is the denominator of the conditional probability and does not change with the slider.

The live label $\mathrm{P}(X>k)$ is the area of the darker region $B$ for the current $k$. At $k=260$ it is about $0.0478$, the numerator. Dividing it by the $\mathrm{P}(X>220)$ reading gives the answer to part a.

scenes.title: Tuning the normal curve to fit both tail conditions
scenes.purpose: Adjust the mean and standard deviation until the area below 180 g is 0.2 and the area above 270 g is 0.05, to see why two equations fix both unknowns.

steps.text: The left tail is $\mathrm{P}(Y<180)$ and should be $0.2$. Since $180$ g is below the mean, $\frac{180-\mu}{\sigma}=-0.8416$. This is the first M1 and part of the B1.
The right tail is $\mathrm{P}(Y>270)=0.05$, so $\mathrm{P}(Y<270)=0.95$ and $\frac{270-\mu}{\sigma}=1.6449$. Using $-1.6449$ or $1.2816$ here is the inverse-normal tail error.
Subtracting $180-\mu=-0.8416\sigma$ from $270-\mu=1.6449\sigma$ gives $90=2.4865\sigma$. The distance of $90$ g between the marks spans $2.4865$ standard deviations, which earns the third M1.

Set $\sigma=36.2$ and $\mu=210.5$: both areas read about $0.2$ and $0.05$. This matches the last M1, $\sigma\approx36.2$ and $\mu\approx210.5$. Try moving either slider and see that one tail is always wrong.

guide.what_you_see: The density curve of the blue cheese mass $Y\sim\mathrm{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)$ with two tails shaded: the area below $180$ g and the area above $270$ g. Two live readings tell you how close those areas are to the required $0.2$ and $0.05$.

legend.meaning: The probability density function of $Y\sim\mathrm{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)$, whose position and width change with your chosen $\mu$ and $\sigma$.
The left-tail area $\mathrm{P}(Y<180)$, which must equal $0.2$ (one wedge in five under $180$ g).
The right-tail area $\mathrm{P}(Y>270)$, which must equal $0.05$ (one wedge in twenty over $270$ g).
The vertical line at $y=180$ g that marks the upper edge of the left tail.
The vertical line at $y=270$ g that marks the lower edge of the right tail.

interact.do: Drag the mean $\mu$ between $180$ and $240$, keeping $\sigma$ fixed, and watch the curve slide sideways.
interact.watch: Moving the curve right makes the left tail bigger or smaller and the right tail change the opposite way, so you cannot fix both tails with $\mu$ alone. At $\mu=210.5$ with $\sigma=36.2$ the readings are about $0.2$ and $0.05$.

interact.do: Drag the standard deviation $\sigma$ between $20$ and $60$, keeping $\mu$ fixed, and watch the curve widen and flatten or narrow and peak.
interact.watch: A larger $\sigma$ moves both tails' areas upward at once, so one slider cannot hit both targets. At $\sigma=36.2$ with $\mu=210.5$ the readings are about $0.2$ and $0.05$.

question_link.text: The shaded area $L$ is the condition $\mathrm{P}(Y<180)=0.2$, giving $\frac{180-\mu}{\sigma}=-0.8416$, and $U$ is $\mathrm{P}(Y>270)=0.05$, giving $\frac{270-\mu}{\sigma}=1.6449$. These are the standardising M1 and the two $z$-values of the B1. Only one pair $(\mu,\sigma)$ meets both conditions, which is why you solve two simultaneous equations.

read_off: The live label for $\mathrm{P}(Y<180)$ gives the area of the left tail for your current $\mu$ and $\sigma$; it should read $0.2$.
The live label for $\mathrm{P}(Y>270)$ gives the area of the right tail for your current $\mu$ and $\sigma$; it should read $0.05$.
